Libya Imposes Temporary Export Restrictions on Crude Oil Shipments

Libya’s Ministry of Oil and Gas has imposed temporary export restrictions on crude oil shipments, a move that has sent ripples through the country’s oil and gas producers. The measure, announced last week, restricts the volume of crude oil allowed for export by 40% per company for the duration of what the ministry described as “critical infrastructure upgrades” at key coastal terminals.

Minister of Oil and Gas Fathi Al-Mansuri stated, “This decision is necessary to ensure the safety and reliability of our export infrastructure, which is undergoing urgent maintenance. We understand the impact on producers, and we are working to minimize the disruption.”

The restrictions, currently in effect at the Es Sider, Ras Lanuf, and Zueitina terminals, have led to a sharp decrease in daily export volumes. Industry data indicates that total crude oil exports from Libya have fallen from an average of 1.1 million barrels per day in May to just over 650,000 barrels per day as of this week.

According to a statement from the Libya Oil Producers Association, “Members are experiencing significant logistical and financial challenges due to the abrupt reduction in export quotas. Storage facilities are nearing capacity, and negotiations with international buyers have become increasingly complicated.”

Mahmoud El-Gharyani, head of strategy at North Sahara Energy, commented, “If the restrictions persist beyond the announced maintenance period, producers may be forced to slow or halt upstream operations, which could have lasting implications for both revenue and production targets.”

Union representatives have expressed concern for workers at impacted facilities. “Our members face uncertainty as production schedules are revised and overtime hours are reduced,” said Amal Farouk, spokesperson for the National Oil Workers Union.

While the ministry has not specified an end date for the restrictions, officials have pledged to review the situation weekly as repairs progress. Producers and industry associations are calling for greater transparency and advanced notice of policy changes.
